# [2301.10521] ExaRanker: Explanation-Augmented Neural Ranker

[View PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2301.10521) [HTML (experimental)](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.10521v2)
> Abstract:Recent work has shown that inducing a large language model (LLM) to generate explanations prior to outputting an answer is an effective strategy to improve performance on a wide range of reasoning tasks. In this work, we show that neural rankers also benefit from explanations. We use LLMs such as GPT-3.5 to augment retrieval datasets with explanations and train a sequence-to-sequence ranking model to output a relevance label and an explanation for a given query-document pair. Our model, dubbed ExaRanker, finetuned on a few thousand examples with synthetic explanations performs on par with models finetuned on 3x more examples without explanations. Furthermore, the ExaRanker model incurs no additional computational cost during ranking and allows explanations to be requested on demand.

# Thiago Laitz

## About

Thiago Laitz developed Exaranker, a neural ranker that uses natural language explanations to rank search results. Laitz is a Research Scientist at Maritaca AI and an Electrical Engineer at Unicamp. They focus on NLP and Information Retrieval, with an emphasis on building Portuguese-language LLMs and efficient ranking systems. Laitz contributed to the Sabiá-3 technical report and created Inranker, a distilled ranking model for zero-shot search. They also developed Bluex, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on Brazilian university entrance exams, and have studied generative models for synthesizing EEG signals in brain-computer interfaces.

## ExperienceUnverified

## Papers23

### Sabiá-3 Technical Report

This report presents Sabi\'a-3, our new flagship language model, and
Sabiazinho-3, a more cost-effective sibling. The models were trained on a large
brazilian-centric corpus. Evaluations across diverse professional and academic
benchmarks show a strong performance on Portuguese and Brazil-related tasks.
Sabi\'a-3 shows large improvements in comparison to our previous best of model,
Sabia-2 Medium, especially in reasoning-intensive tasks. Notably, Sabi\'a-3's
average performance matches frontier LLMs, while it is offered at a three to
four times lower cost per token, reinforcing the benefits of domain
specialization.

### ExaRanker: Explanation-Augmented Neural Ranker

Recent work has shown that inducing a large language model (LLM) to generate explanations prior to outputting an answer is an effective strategy to improve performance on a wide range of reasoning tasks. In this work, we show that neural rankers also benefit from explanations. We use LLMs such as GPT-3.5 to augment retrieval datasets with explanations and train a sequence-to-sequence ranking model to output a relevance label and an explanation for a given query-document pair. Our model, dubbed ExaRanker, finetuned on a few thousand examples with synthetic explanations performs on par with models finetuned on 3x more examples without explanations. Furthermore, the ExaRanker model incurs no additional computational cost during ranking and allows explanations to be requested on demand.

### BLUEX: A benchmark based on Brazilian Leading Universities Entrance eXams

One common trend in recent studies of language models (LMs) is the use of standardized tests for evaluation. However, despite being the fifth most spoken language worldwide, few such evaluations have been conducted in Portuguese. This is mainly due to the lack of high-quality datasets available to the community for carrying out evaluations in Portuguese. To address this gap, we introduce the Brazilian Leading Universities Entrance eXams (BLUEX), a dataset of entrance exams from the two leading universities in Brazil: UNICAMP and USP. The dataset includes annotated metadata for evaluating the performance of NLP models on a variety of subjects. Furthermore, BLUEX includes a collection of recently administered exams that are unlikely to be included in the training data of many popular LMs as of 2023. The dataset is also annotated to indicate the position of images in each question, providing a valuable resource for advancing the state-of-the-art in multimodal language understanding and reasoning. We describe the creation and characteristics of BLUEX and establish a benchmark through experiments with state-of-the-art LMs, demonstrating its potential for advancing the state-of-the-art in natural language understanding and reasoning in Portuguese. The data and relevant code can be found at this https URL

### InRanker: Distilled Rankers for Zero-shot Information Retrieval

Despite multi-billion parameter neural rankers being common components of
state-of-the-art information retrieval pipelines, they are rarely used in
production due to the enormous amount of compute required for inference. In
this work, we propose a new method for distilling large rankers into their
smaller versions focusing on out-of-domain effectiveness. We introduce
InRanker, a version of monoT5 distilled from monoT5-3B with increased
effectiveness on out-of-domain scenarios. Our key insight is to use language
models and rerankers to generate as much as possible synthetic "in-domain"
training data, i.e., data that closely resembles the data that will be seen at
retrieval time. The pipeline consists of two distillation phases that do not
require additional user queries or manual annotations: (1) training on existing
supervised soft teacher labels, and (2) training on teacher soft labels for
synthetic queries generated using a large language model. Consequently, models
like monoT5-60M and monoT5-220M improved their effectiveness by using the
teacher's knowledge, despite being 50x and 13x smaller, respectively. Models
and code are available at https://github.com/unicamp-dl/InRanker.

### Sabiá-4 Technical Report

This technical report presents Sabiá-4 and Sabiazinho-4, a new generation of Portuguese language models with a focus on Brazilian Portuguese language. The models were developed through a four-stage training pipeline: continued pre-training on Portuguese and Brazilian legal corpora, long-context extension to 128K tokens, supervised fine-tuning on instruction data spanning chat, code, legal tasks, and function calling, and preference alignment. We evaluate the models on six benchmark categories: conversational capabilities in Brazilian Portuguese, knowledge of Brazilian legislation, long-context understanding, instruction following, standardized exams, and agentic capabilities including tool use and web navigation. Results show that Sabiá-4 and Sabiazinho-4 achieve a favorable cost-performance trade-off compared to other models, positioning them in the upper-left region of the pricing-accuracy chart. The models show improvements over previous generations in legal document drafting, multi-turn dialogue quality, and agentic task completion.

### Measuring Opinion Bias and Sycophancy via LLM-based Persuasion

Large language models increasingly shape the information people consume: they are embedded in search, consulted for professional advice, deployed as agents, and used as a first stop for questions about policy, ethics, health, and politics. When such a model silently holds a position on a contested topic, that position propagates at scale into users' decisions. Eliciting a model's positions is harder than it first appears: contemporary assistants answer direct opinion questions with evasive disclaimers, and the same model may concede the opposite position once the user starts arguing one side. We propose a method, released as the open-source llm-bias-bench, for discovering the opinions an LLM actually holds on contested topics under conditions that resemble real multi-turn interaction. The method pairs two complementary free-form probes. Direct probing asks for the model's opinion across five turns of escalating pressure from a simulated user. Indirect probing never asks for an opinion and engages the model in argumentative debate, letting bias leak through how it concedes, resists, or counter-argues. Three user personas (neutral, agree, disagree) collapse into a nine-way behavioral classification that separates persona-independent positions from persona-dependent sycophancy, and an auditable LLM judge produces verdicts with textual evidence. The first instantiation ships 38 topics in Brazilian Portuguese across values, scientific consensus, philosophy, and economic policy. Applied to 13 assistants, the method surfaces findings of practical interest: argumentative debate triggers sycophancy 2-3x more than direct questioning (median 50% to 79%); models that look opinionated under direct questioning often collapse into mirroring under sustained arguments; and attacker capability matters mainly when an existing opinion must be dislodged, not when the assistant starts neutral.

### NeuralSearchX: Serving a Multi-billion-parameter Reranker for Multilingual Metasearch at a Low Cost

The widespread availability of search API's (both free and commercial) brings the promise of increased coverage and quality of search results for metasearch engines, while decreasing the maintenance costs of the crawling and indexing infrastructures. However, merging strategies frequently comprise complex pipelines that require careful tuning, which is often overlooked in the literature. In this work, we describe NeuralSearchX, a metasearch engine based on a multi-purpose large reranking model to merge results and highlight sentences. Due to the homogeneity of our architecture, we could focus our optimization efforts on a single component. We compare our system with Microsoft's Biomedical Search and show that our design choices led to a much cost-effective system with competitive QPS while having close to state-of-the-art results on a wide range of public benchmarks. Human evaluation on two domain-specific tasks shows that our retrieval system outperformed Google API by a large margin in terms of nDCG@10 scores. By describing our architecture and implementation in detail, we hope that the community will build on our design choices. The system is available at this https URL.

### Ticket-Bench: A Kickoff for Multilingual and Regionalized Agent Evaluation

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as task-oriented agents, where success depends on their ability to generate accurate function calls under realistic, multilingual conditions. However, existing agent evaluations largely overlook cultural and linguistic diversity, often relying on monolingual or naively translated benchmarks. We introduce Ticket-Bench, a benchmark for multilingual agent evaluation in task-oriented scenarios. Ticket-Bench simulates the domain of soccer ticket purchases across six major languages: Portuguese, English, Spanish, German, Italian, and French. Using localized teams, cities, and user profiles to provide a higher level of realism. We evaluate a wide range of commercial and open-source LLMs, measuring function-calling accuracy and consistency across languages. Results show that reasoning-oriented models (e.g., GPT-5, Qwen3-235B) dominate performance but still exhibit notable cross-lingual disparities. These findings underscore the need for culturally aware, multilingual benchmarks to guide the development of robust LLM agents.

### Magis-Bench: Evaluating LLMs on Magistrate-Level Legal Tasks

Existing benchmarks for legal AI focus primarily on tasks where LLMs must produce legal arguments or documents, yet the capacity to *judge* such arguments -- weighing competing claims, applying doctrine to facts, and rendering reasoned decisions -- is arguably as fundamental to a well-functioning legal system as advocacy itself. We introduce Magis-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on magistrate-level writing tasks derived from recent Brazilian competitive examinations for judicial positions. Magis-Bench comprises 74 questions from eight examinations conducted between 2023 and 2025, including discursive legal analysis questions with multi-turn structure and practical exercises requiring the composition of complete civil and criminal judicial sentences. We evaluate 23 state-of-the-art LLMs using an LLM-as-a-judge methodology with four independent frontier models as evaluators. Our results show strong inter-judge agreement (Kendall's <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.984</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W = 0.984</annotation></semantics></math> --> W=0.984W = 0.984; pairwise Kendall's <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>0.897</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau \ge 0.897</annotation></semantics></math> --> τ≥0.897\tau \ge 0.897), with Google's Gemini-3-Pro-Preview achieving the highest average score (6.97/10), followed by Gemini-3-Flash-Preview (6.67) and Claude-4.5-Opus (6.46). Even the best-performing models score below 70% of the maximum, indicating that judicial-level legal reasoning and writing remain challenging for current LLMs. We release the complete benchmark, model outputs, and evaluation code to support further research on legal AI capabilities.

### SurveySum: A Dataset for Summarizing Multiple Scientific Articles into a Survey Section

Leandro Carísio FernandesGustavo Bartz Guedes[![Thiago Soares Laitz](https://proxy.assets.alphaxiv.org/aHR0cHM6Ly9zY2hvbGFyLmdvb2dsZXVzZXJjb250ZW50LmNvbS9jaXRhdGlvbnM_dmlld19vcD12aWV3X3Bob3RvJnVzZXI9SjJkNkxxRUFBQUFKJmNpdHBpZD03)Thiago Soares Laitz](https://www.alphaxiv.org/@thiago-laitz)[![Thales Sales Almeida](https://proxy.assets.alphaxiv.org/aHR0cHM6Ly9zY2hvbGFyLmdvb2dsZXVzZXJjb250ZW50LmNvbS9jaXRhdGlvbnM_dmlld19vcD12aWV3X3Bob3RvJnVzZXI9R0ZaNWl6OEFBQUFKJmNpdHBpZD0y)Thales Sales Almeida](https://www.alphaxiv.org/@thales-sales-almeida)+3

Document summarization is a task to shorten texts into concise and informative summaries. This paper introduces a novel dataset designed for summarizing multiple scientific articles into a section of a survey. Our contributions are: (1) SurveySum, a new dataset addressing the gap in domain-specific summarization tools; (2) two specific pipelines to summarize scientific articles into a section of a survey; and (3) the evaluation of these pipelines using multiple metrics to compare their performance. Our results highlight the importance of high-quality retrieval stages and the impact of different configurations on the quality of generated summaries.

pergunta: Você pode listar todos os secretários de Transportes dos EUA do início de 2018 até o fim de 2024, incluindo secretários interinos?
resposta:
Com base nas informações verificadas nos registros oficiais do Departamento de Transporte dos EUA e na Wikipédia, aqui está a lista completa dos Secretários de Transportes dos Estados Unidos no período de **início de 2018 até o fim de 2024**, incluindo interinos:

---

## Período de 2018–2024

### 1. Elaine Chao — Secretária titular
| | |
|---|---|
| **Cargo** | 18ª Secretária de Transportes (titular) |
| **Início do mandato** | 31 de janeiro de 2017 |
| **Fim do mandato** | 11 de janeiro de 2021 (resignou após os protestos de 6 de janeiro) |
| **Cobertura no período pedido** | ✅ Toda a década solicitada (jan/2018 – dez/2024) |
| **Observações** | Foi confirmada pelo Senado em 31 de janeiro de 2017. Serviu sem interrupções durante todo o período de 2018 a 2020, passando pelos governos Trump e início de Biden. Não houve nenhum secretário interino durante sua posse no período analisado. |

### 2. Pete Buttigieg — Secretário titular
| | |
|---|---|
| **Cargo** | 19º Secretário de Transportes (titular) |
| **Início do mandato** | 3 de fevereiro de 2021 |
| **Fim do mandato (no período)** | 31 de dezembro de 2024 |
| **Observações** | Confirmado pelo Senado em 2 de fevereiro de 2021 (voto histórico de 86–13). Tomou posse como o membro de gabinete mais jovem da administração Biden e permaneceu no cargo **sem qualquer substituto interino ou designação temporária** por todo o período de 2021 até dezembro de 2024, quando já se aguardava sua saída (que ocorreu oficialmente em 20 de janeiro de 2025, já fora do recorte solicitado). |

---

## Resumo

No período de **janeiro de 2018 a dezembro de 2024**, os únicos Secretários de Transportes dos EUA foram:

| # | Secretário | Período exato no escopo pedido | Tipo |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Elaine Chao** | jan/2018 – jan/2021 (até sair) | Titular |
| 2 | **Pete Buttigieg** | fev/2021 – dez/2024 | Titular |

**Não houve nenhum secretário interino ou substituto temporário nesse intervalo.** As únicas trocas no posto que ocorreram próximas ao período foram:
- **Steven G. Bradbury** (interino): 12–20 de janeiro de 2021 (antes de Buttigieg tomar posse oficial);
- **Lana Hurdle** (interina): 20 de janeiro – 3 de fevereiro de 2021 (breve transição, também antes de Buttigieg assumir formalmente).

Portanto, dentro do recorte solicitado (início de 2018 até fim de 2024), não há lacunas com interinos — apenas dois secretários titulares consecutivos servindo sem interrupção.

Fonte: [Wikipedia – United States Secretary of Transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation) e [DOT Archives & History – Dates of Service](https://transportation.libguides.com/c.php?g=1154894&p=8445303).

checklist: O relatório deve mencionar que Elaine Chao foi secretária de Transportes no período.
O relatório deve mencionar que Steven G. Bradbury foi secretário de Transportes no período.
O relatório deve mencionar que Lana Hurdle foi secretária de Transportes no período.
O relatório deve mencionar que Pete Buttigieg foi secretário de Transportes no período.

check_items.explanation: O relatório menciona claramente Elaine Chao como secretária titular de Transportes dos EUA, incluindo as datas corretas de exercício (até 11 de janeiro de 2021).

Steven G. Bradbury é citado na seção de Resumo, mas o relatório diz que seu breve exercício interino (12–20 de janeiro de 2021) foi "próximo ao período", sugerindo que não está dentro do recorte solicitado. Contudo, considerando a data pedida (até o fim de 2024, cobrindo inclusive janeiro de 2021), Bradbury serviu entre o final de Chao e a posse de Buttigieg, sendo correto mencioná-lo. Portanto, Bradbury foi corretamente citado, embora com dúvida se pertence "dentro do intervalo principal".

Lana Hurdle também é mencionada na seção de Resumo como secretária interina de 20 de janeiro a 3 de fevereiro de 2021, ou seja, durante parte do período solicitado. O nome, período e a função como interina estão presentes.
Pete Buttigieg é amplamente destacado no relatório, com datas detalhadas de início de mandato e funções. Está correta a identificação do período de exercício dentro do escopo pedido.

The **United States secretary of transportation** is the head of the [United States Department of Transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Transportation "United States Department of Transportation"). The secretary serves as the principal advisor to the [president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") on all matters relating to transportation. The secretary is a statutory member of the [Cabinet of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States"), and is fourteenth in the [presidential line of succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_line_of_succession "United States presidential line of succession").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-code-1)

The secretary of transportation oversees the U.S. Department of Transportation, which has over 55,000 employees and [thirteen agencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Transportation#Agencies "United States Department of Transportation"), including the [Federal Aviation Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Aviation_Administration "Federal Aviation Administration"), the [Federal Highway Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Highway_Administration "Federal Highway Administration"), the [Federal Railroad Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Railroad_Administration "Federal Railroad Administration"), and the [National Highway Traffic Safety Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Highway_Traffic_Safety_Administration "National Highway Traffic Safety Administration").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-DOTHist-2) As of January 2021, the secretary receives an annual salary of $221,400.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-Salary-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-4)

[Sean Duffy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Duffy "Sean Duffy") has served as the 20th secretary of transportation since January 28, 2025. He was appointed by President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") to serve this position, and was confirmed by the [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") in a 77-22 vote.

## History

The post was created on October 15, 1966, by the Department of Transportation Act, signed into law by President [Lyndon B. Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyndon_B._Johnson "Lyndon B. Johnson").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-DOTHist-2) The department's mission is "to develop and coordinate policies that will provide an efficient and economical national transportation system, with due regard for need, the environment, and the national defense."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-DOTHist-2)

The first secretary of transportation was [Alan S. Boyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_S._Boyd "Alan S. Boyd"), nominated to the post by Democratic president Lyndon B. Johnson. [Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan")'s second secretary of transportation, [Elizabeth Dole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Dole "Elizabeth Dole"), was the first female holder, and Mary Peters was the second. [Gerald Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Ford "Gerald Ford")'s nominee [William Thaddeus Coleman Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Thaddeus_Coleman_Jr. "William Thaddeus Coleman Jr.") was the first African American to serve as transportation secretary, and [Federico Peña](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federico_Peña "Federico Peña"), serving under [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton"), was the first Hispanic to hold the position, subsequently becoming the [secretary of energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_Energy "Secretary of Energy"). Japanese-American [Norman Mineta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Mineta "Norman Mineta"), who had previously been the [secretary of commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_Commerce "Secretary of Commerce"), is the longest-serving secretary, holding the post for over five and a half years,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-DOTHist-2) and [Andrew Card](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Card "Andrew Card") is the shortest-serving secretary, serving only eleven months. [Pete Buttigieg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg "Pete Buttigieg") is the youngest secretary, taking office at 39 years 15 days old, overtaking [Neil Goldschmidt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Goldschmidt "Neil Goldschmidt") as the youngest secretary, taking office at 39 years 3 months old,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-CNBC-5) while Norman Mineta was the oldest, retiring at age 74.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-DOTBio-6) Buttigieg is also the first openly [gay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gay "Gay") man to hold the position, as well as being the first openly gay Cabinet secretary, and the first to seek a full senate confirmation.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-7) In April 2008, [Mary Peters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_E._Peters "Mary E. Peters") launched the official blog of the secretary of transportation called *The Fast Lane*.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-8) On January 23, 2009, the 16th secretary, [Ray LaHood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_LaHood "Ray LaHood"), took office, serving under the administration of Democrat [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama"); he had previously been a Republican congressman from Illinois for fourteen years.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-9)

[Anthony Foxx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Foxx "Anthony Foxx") was the 17th U.S. secretary of transportation from 2013 to 2017, when [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") was president. [Elaine Chao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Chao "Elaine Chao"), who served as the [secretary of labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Labor "United States Secretary of Labor") under President [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush"), was nominated by [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") on November 29, 2016. On January 31, 2017, the Senate confirmed her appointment by a vote of 93–6. On January 7, 2021, Chao announced her resignation following the [January 6 United States Capitol attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/January_6_United_States_Capitol_attack "January 6 United States Capitol attack"), effective January 11.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-10) On January 11, 2021, acting [deputy secretary of transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Deputy_Secretary_of_Transportation "United States Deputy Secretary of Transportation") [Steven G. Bradbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_G._Bradbury "Steven G. Bradbury") became acting secretary of transportation. Pete Buttigieg served as the 19th secretary of transportation during the presidency of [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden").

## Line of succession

The [line of succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_of_succession "Line of succession") regarding who would act as Secretary of Transportation in the event of a vacancy or incapacitation is as follows:[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation#cite_note-14)

1. [Deputy Secretary of Transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deputy_Secretary_of_Transportation "Deputy Secretary of Transportation")
2. [Under Secretary of Transportation for Policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Under_Secretary_of_Transportation_for_Policy "Under Secretary of Transportation for Policy")
3. General Counsel
4. Assistant Secretary for Budget and Programs
5. Assistant Secretary for Transportation Policy
6. Assistant Secretary for Governmental Affairs
7. Assistant Secretary for Aviation and International Affairs
8. Assistant Secretary for Administration
9. Administrator of the [Federal Highway Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Highway_Administration "Federal Highway Administration")
10. Administrator of the [Federal Aviation Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Aviation_Administration "Federal Aviation Administration")
11. Administrator of the [Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Motor_Carrier_Safety_Administration "Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration")
12. Administrator of the [Federal Railroad Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Railroad_Administration "Federal Railroad Administration")
13. Administrator of the [Federal Transit Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Transit_Administration "Federal Transit Administration")
14. Administrator of the [Maritime Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Maritime_Administration "United States Maritime Administration")
15. Administrator of the [Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pipeline_and_Hazardous_Materials_Safety_Administration "Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration")
16. Administrator of the [National Highway Traffic Safety Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Highway_Traffic_Safety_Administration "National Highway Traffic Safety Administration")
17. Administrator of the [Research and Innovative Technology Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_and_Innovative_Technology_Administration "Research and Innovative Technology Administration")
18. Administrator of the [Great Lakes St. Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Lakes_St._Lawrence_Seaway_Development_Corporation "Great Lakes St. Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation")
19. Regional Administrator, Southern Region, Federal Aviation Administration
20. Director, Resource Center, Lakewood, Colorado, Federal Highway Administration
21. Regional Administrator, Northwest Mountain Region, Federal Aviation Administration

**Peter Paul Montgomery Buttigieg** ([/ˈbuːtɪdʒədʒ/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English") [https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/3/3b/En-us-Buttigieg-2.ogg/En-us-Buttigieg-2.ogg.mp3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/3/3b/En-us-Buttigieg-2.ogg/En-us-Buttigieg-2.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:En-us-Buttigieg-2.ogg "File:En-us-Buttigieg-2.ogg") [*BOO-tij-əj*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key");[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-3) born January 19, 1982) is an American politician and former [naval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy "United States Navy") officer who served as the 19th [United States secretary of transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation "United States Secretary of Transportation") from 2021 to 2025. A member of the [Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)"), he previously served as the 32nd [mayor of South Bend, Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_mayors_of_South_Bend,_Indiana "List of mayors of South Bend, Indiana"), from 2012 to 2020.

Buttigieg is a graduate of [Harvard College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_College "Harvard College") and the [University of Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford"), attending the latter on a [Rhodes Scholarship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodes_Scholarship "Rhodes Scholarship"). In 2007, he began three years of work at the [management consulting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Management_consulting "Management consulting") firm [McKinsey & Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McKinsey_&_Company "McKinsey & Company"). From 2009 to 2017, he was an [intelligence officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_Naval_Intelligence "Office of Naval Intelligence") in the [United States Navy Reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy_Reserve "United States Navy Reserve"), attaining the rank of [lieutenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieutenant_(navy) "Lieutenant (navy)"). He was mobilized and [deployed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_deployment#United_States "Military deployment") to the [war in Afghanistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_in_Afghanistan_(2001–2021) "War in Afghanistan (2001–2021)") for seven months in 2014. Afterwards, he worked on the political campaigns of Democrats [Jill Long Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jill_Long_Thompson "Jill Long Thompson"), [Joe Donnelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Donnelly "Joe Donnelly"), and [John Kerry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kerry "John Kerry"), and was the unsuccessful Democratic nominee for [Indiana state treasurer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_State_Treasurer "Indiana State Treasurer") in [2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Indiana_State_Treasurer_election "2010 Indiana State Treasurer election"). In [2011](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_South_Bend_mayoral_election "2011 South Bend mayoral election"), he was elected mayor of South Bend. In [2015](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_South_Bend_mayoral_election "2015 South Bend mayoral election"), Buttigieg was re-elected, [coming out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coming_out "Coming out") as gay earlier that year. He married [Chasten Glezman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chasten_Buttigieg "Chasten Buttigieg"), a schoolteacher and writer, in June 2018. Buttigieg declined to seek a third term as mayor.

In April 2019, Buttigieg announced a [2020 presidential campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg_2020_presidential_campaign "Pete Buttigieg 2020 presidential campaign"), making him the first openly gay man to launch a Democratic presidential campaign.[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-5) During the [Democratic Party primaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Democratic_Party_presidential_primaries "2020 Democratic Party presidential primaries"), he gained significant momentum in mid-2019 after several [town hall meetings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Town_hall_meeting "Town hall meeting") and [television debates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Democratic_Party_presidential_debates "2020 Democratic Party presidential debates"). Buttigieg narrowly won the [Iowa caucuses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Iowa_Democratic_caucuses "2020 Iowa Democratic caucuses") while placing second in the popular vote, and placed a close second in the [New Hampshire primary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_New_Hampshire_Democratic_primary "2020 New Hampshire Democratic primary").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-6)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Nilsen-2020-7)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-8) By winning Iowa, he became the first openly gay candidate to win a presidential primary or caucus. Buttigieg dropped out of the race on March 1, 2020, and endorsed [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") the following day.

After Biden won the [2020 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election "2020 United States presidential election"), he named Buttigieg as his nominee for Secretary of Transportation in December 2020. His nomination was confirmed on February 2, 2021, by a vote of 86–13, making him the first openly gay Cabinet secretary in U.S. history.[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-11) Nominated at age 38, he was also the youngest Cabinet member in the [Biden administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_Joe_Biden "Cabinet of Joe Biden") and the youngest person ever to serve as Secretary of Transportation. After Biden withdrew his re-election campaign in 2024, Buttigieg was considered as a [potential running mate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Democratic_Party_vice_presidential_candidate_selection "2024 Democratic Party vice presidential candidate selection") for [Kamala Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamala_Harris "Kamala Harris"), though he was ultimately not selected.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-12)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-13)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-14)

## Early life and career

Pete Buttigieg was born on January 19, 1982, in [South Bend, Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Bend,_Indiana "South Bend, Indiana"), to Jennifer "Anne" Montgomery and [Joseph Anthony Buttigieg II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Anthony_Buttigieg_II "Joseph Anthony Buttigieg II").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-15)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-16)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Gabriel-2020-17)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-18) He is an only child. His parents met and married while employed as faculty at [New Mexico State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Mexico_State_University "New Mexico State University").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-19) His father was born in [Ħamrun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamrun "Hamrun"), [Malta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malta "Malta"), and emigrated to the United States to pursue his doctorate.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-20)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Laviola-21) Buttigieg's father embarked on a career as a professor of English at the [University of Notre Dame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Notre_Dame "University of Notre Dame") near South Bend.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Laviola-21)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Trebay-2018-22) Buttigieg's mother also taught at the University of Notre Dame for 29 years.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-23) His father, a translator of Italian Marxist philosopher [Antonio Gramsci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_Gramsci "Antonio Gramsci")'s *[Prison Notebooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prison_Notebooks "Prison Notebooks")* and the editor of a three-volume English edition, influenced his son's decision to study literature in college.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-24)

### Education

Buttigieg was [valedictorian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valedictorian "Valedictorian") of the class of 2000 at [St. Joseph High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_High_School_(South_Bend,_Indiana) "St. Joseph High School (South Bend, Indiana)") in South Bend.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-25)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-26) That year, he won first prize in the [John F. Kennedy Presidential Library and Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy_Presidential_Library_and_Museum "John F. Kennedy Presidential Library and Museum")'s *Profiles in Courage* essay contest. He traveled to Boston where he accepted the award and met [Caroline Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caroline_Kennedy "Caroline Kennedy") and other members of the [Kennedy family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_family "Kennedy family"). The subject of his essay was the integrity and political courage of then [U.S. representative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") [Bernie Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernie_Sanders "Bernie Sanders") of [Vermont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vermont "Vermont"), one of only two [independent politicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_politician "Independent politician") in Congress.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-27)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-28)[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-30)

In 2000, Buttigieg was one of two students chosen to be a delegate from Indiana to the [United States Senate Youth Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Youth_Program "United States Senate Youth Program"),[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-31) an annual scholarship competition sponsored jointly by the [U.S. Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate "U.S. Senate") and the Hearst Foundations.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-32) In his last high-school year, Buttigieg was named the school valedictorian, voted senior class president and chosen Most Likely to be U.S. President.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-33)

After graduating from high school, Buttigieg attended [Harvard College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_College "Harvard College"), where he majored in history and literature.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-34) He became president of the Student Advisory Committee of the [Harvard Institute of Politics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Institute_of_Politics "Harvard Institute of Politics") and worked on the institute's annual study of youth attitudes on politics.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Harvard_Institute_of_Politics-2012-35)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-36) His undergraduate thesis, *The Quiet American's Errand into the Wilderness*, examined the influence of [Puritanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puritanism "Puritanism") on U.S. foreign policy as reflected in [Graham Greene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graham_Greene "Graham Greene")'s novel *[The Quiet American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Quiet_American "The Quiet American")*.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-37)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-38) He graduated *[magna cum laude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magna_cum_laude "Magna cum laude")* from Harvard in 2004, and was elected a member of [Phi Beta Kappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phi_Beta_Kappa "Phi Beta Kappa").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Harvard_Gazette-2004-39)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-40)

Buttigieg was awarded a [Rhodes Scholarship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodes_Scholarship "Rhodes Scholarship") to study at the [University of Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Harvard_Gazette-2004-39)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-41) In 2007, he received a [Bachelor of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") degree with [first-class honours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_undergraduate_degree_classification#First-class_honours "British undergraduate degree classification") in [philosophy, politics, and economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophy,_politics,_and_economics "Philosophy, politics, and economics") after studying at [Pembroke College, Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pembroke_College,_Oxford "Pembroke College, Oxford").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Wallace-Wells-2019-42)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-43)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-44)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-45) At Oxford, he was an editor of the *Oxford International Review*,[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Times-Union-2010-46) and was a co-founder[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Times-Union-2010-46) and member of the Democratic Renaissance Project, an informal debate and discussion group of approximately a dozen Oxford students.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-47)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-48)

### Professional career

Before graduating from college, Buttigieg was an investigative intern at [WMAQ-TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WMAQ-TV "WMAQ-TV"), Chicago's [NBC News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC_News "NBC News") affiliate.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-49) He also interned for Democrat [Jill Long Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jill_Long_Thompson "Jill Long Thompson") during her unsuccessful [2002 congressional bid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections_in_Indiana#District_2 "2002 United States House of Representatives elections in Indiana").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-50)

After college, Buttigieg worked on [John Kerry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kerry "John Kerry")'s [2004 presidential campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kerry_presidential_campaign,_2004 "John Kerry presidential campaign, 2004") as a policy and research specialist for several months in [Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona "Arizona") and [New Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Mexico "New Mexico").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-51)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-52) From 2004 to 2005, Buttigieg was conference director of the Cohen Group.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-53) In 2006, he lent assistance to [Joe Donnelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Donnelly "Joe Donnelly")'s successful [congressional campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections_in_Indiana#District_2 "2006 United States House of Representatives elections in Indiana").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-54)

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/Pete_Afghanistan_5.jpg_large.jpg/250px-Pete_Afghanistan_5.jpg_large.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pete_Afghanistan_5.jpg_large.jpg)Buttigieg in 2014 during his service in Afghanistan

After earning his Oxford degree, in 2007, Buttigieg became a consultant at the Chicago office of [McKinsey & Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McKinsey_&_Company "McKinsey & Company"),[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Wang-2019-55)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-56) where he worked on energy, retail, economic development, and logistics for three years.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Truman_National_Security_Project-57)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-58) His clients at McKinsey included the [health insurer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_insurance_in_the_United_States "Health insurance in the United States") [Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Cross_Blue_Shield_of_Michigan "Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan"); electronics retailer [Best Buy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best_Buy "Best Buy"); Canadian supermarket chain [Loblaws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loblaws "Loblaws"); two nonprofit environmentalist groups, the [Natural Resources Defense Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Resources_Defense_Council "Natural Resources Defense Council") and Energy Foundation; and several U.S. government agencies, the [Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Environmental_Protection_Agency "United States Environmental Protection Agency"), [Energy Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Energy "United States Department of Energy"), [Defense Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense"), and [Postal Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Postal_Service "United States Postal Service").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-59)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-60) He took a leave of absence from McKinsey in 2008 to become research director for Jill Long Thompson's unsuccessful [campaign for Indiana governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Indiana_gubernatorial_election "2008 Indiana gubernatorial election").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-61)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-62)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-63) His work at McKinsey included trips to Iraq and Afghanistan, which he rarely discusses.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-64) Buttigieg left McKinsey in 2010 in order to focus full-time on his campaign for Indiana state treasurer.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Wang-2019-55)

Buttigieg has been involved with the [Truman National Security Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truman_National_Security_Project "Truman National Security Project") since 2005 and serves as a fellow with expertise in Afghanistan and Pakistan.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Truman_National_Security_Project-57) He was named to the organization's board of advisors in 2014.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-65)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Harvard_Institute_of_Politics-2012-35)

### Military service

Buttigieg joined the [U.S. Navy Reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Navy_Reserve "U.S. Navy Reserve") through the [direct commission officer (DCO)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_commission_officer "Direct commission officer") program and was sworn in as an [ensign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ensign_(rank) "Ensign (rank)") in naval intelligence in September 2009.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-66) He took a seven-month leave during his mayoral term to deploy to Afghanistan in 2014.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-67)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-68)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-69)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-70) While there, Buttigieg was part of a unit assigned to identify and disrupt terrorist finance networks. Part of this was done at [Bagram Air Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bagram_Air_Base "Bagram Air Base"), but he was also an armed driver for his commander on more than 100 trips into [Kabul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kabul "Kabul"), where he was tasked with watching out for ambushes and explosive devices along the roads and ensuring that the vehicle was guarded. Buttigieg has jokingly referred to this role as "military [Uber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uber "Uber")".[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-71) Also, while deployed in Afghanistan, Buttigieg was assigned to the [Afghan Threat Finance Cell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan_Threat_Finance_Cell "Afghan Threat Finance Cell"), a [counterterrorism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterterrorism "Counterterrorism") unit that targeted [Taliban insurgency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taliban_insurgency "Taliban insurgency") financing.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-72)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-73) Buttigieg was awarded the [Joint Service Commendation Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Service_Commendation_Medal "Joint Service Commendation Medal").[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-74) He left the U.S. Navy Reserve in 2017.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-75)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-76)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-77)

### Indiana state treasurer election

Main article: [2010 Indiana State Treasurer election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Indiana_State_Treasurer_election "2010 Indiana State Treasurer election")

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ef/PeteButtigieg.JPG/250px-PeteButtigieg.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:PeteButtigieg.JPG)Buttigieg campaign photo for [Indiana State Treasurer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_State_Treasurer "Indiana State Treasurer") in March 2010

Buttigieg was the [Democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") nominee for [state treasurer of Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_State_Treasurer "Indiana State Treasurer") in 2010. He received 37.5 percent of the vote, losing to [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") incumbent [Richard Mourdock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Mourdock "Richard Mourdock").[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-78)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-79) Much of Buttigieg's campaign had focused on criticizing Mourdock for investing state [pension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pension "Pension") funds in [Chrysler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chrysler "Chrysler") [junk bonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junk_bonds "Junk bonds"), and for having subsequently filed a lawsuit against [Chrysler's bankruptcy restructuring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chrysler_Chapter_11_reorganization "Chrysler Chapter 11 reorganization"), which Buttigieg argued imperiled Chrysler jobs in the state of Indiana.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-80)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-81)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-82)

## Mayor of South Bend

Main article: [Mayoralty of Pete Buttigieg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayoralty_of_Pete_Buttigieg "Mayoralty of Pete Buttigieg")

### First term

Buttigieg ran for the Democratic nomination for [mayor of South Bend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_mayors_of_South_Bend,_Indiana "List of mayors of South Bend, Indiana") in 2011. In a [PBS Michiana – WNIT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WNIT_(TV) "WNIT (TV)") broadcast, he expressed his desire to reinvigorate South Bend, especially with respect to job creation and education.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-83) Buttigieg campaigned on other issues, such as pursuing international investment,[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-84) increasing presence of police and other safety professionals,[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-85) and improving city services.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-86) Buttigieg won his primary election against four opponents on May 3, 2011, receiving 7,663 votes.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-87) Buttigieg was elected mayor of South Bend in the [November 2011 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_South_Bend_mayoral_election "2011 South Bend mayoral election") with 10,991 of the 14,883 votes cast, or 74 percent of all votes.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Fuller-2014-88) He defeated Republican nominee Norris W. Curry Jr. and [Libertarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libertarian_Party_(United_States) "Libertarian Party (United States)") nominee Patrick M. Farrell.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-89) Buttigieg took office in January 2012 at the age of 29, becoming the second-youngest mayor in South Bend history[[e]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-91) and the youngest incumbent mayor, at the time, of a U.S. city with at least 100,000 residents.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Fuller-2014-88)

After a federal investigation ruled that South Bend police had illegally recorded telephone calls of several officers, Buttigieg demoted [police chief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_of_police "Chief of police") Darryl Boykins in 2012.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-South_Bend_Tribune-2018-92)[[f]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-94) Buttigieg also dismissed the department's communications director, who had discovered the recordings but continued to record the line at Boykins's command.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-South_Bend_Tribune-2018-92) The police communications director alleged that the recordings captured four senior police officers making racist remarks and discussing illegal acts.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-South_Bend_Tribune-2018-92)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Buckley-95)

Buttigieg has written that his "first serious mistake as mayor" came shortly after taking office in 2012, when he decided to ask for Boykins's resignation. Backed by supporters and legal counsel, Boykins requested reinstatement. When Buttigieg denied his request, Boykins, as the city's first African American police chief, sued the city for racial discrimination,[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-96) arguing that the taping policy had existed under previous police chiefs, who were white.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Easley-2019-97) Buttigieg settled the lawsuits brought by Boykins and the four officers out of court for over $800,000.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-South_Bend_Tribune-2018-92)[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-98) A federal judge ruled in 2015 that Boykins's recordings violated the [Federal Wiretap Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_Communications_Privacy_Act "Electronic Communications Privacy Act").[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Buckley-95) Buttigieg came under pressure from political opponents to release the eight tapes, but he said that it was not possible to release seven of them, citing the Federal Wiretap Act.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-South_Bend_Tribune-2018-92)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Buckley-95) It was unclear if releasing the eighth tape would violate any laws.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Buckley-95) [St. Joseph County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph_County,_Indiana "St. Joseph County, Indiana") Superior Court Judge Steve Hostetler heard a case for the release of five cassette tapes.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Easley-2019-97) Judge Hostetler ruled that the cassette tapes must be released to the South Bend City Council in May 2021.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-99)

As mayor, Buttigieg promoted a number of development and redevelopment projects.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-100) Buttigieg was a leading figure behind the creation of a nightly laser-light display along downtown South Bend's St. Joseph River trail as public art. The project cost $700,000, which was raised from private funds.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Sikich-2019-101) The "River Lights" installation was unveiled in May 2015 as part of the city's 150th anniversary celebrations.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-South_Bend_Tribune-2018-92) He also oversaw the city's launching of a [3-1-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3-1-1 "3-1-1") system in 2013.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-southbendvoice-102)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-103) Buttigieg's administration oversaw the sale of numerous city-owned properties.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-104)[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-105)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-106)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-107) One of Buttigieg's signature programs was the "Vacant and Abandoned Properties Initiative". Known locally as *1,000 Properties in 1,000 Days*, it was a project to repair or demolish blighted properties across South Bend.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-108)[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-109) The program reached its goal two months before its scheduled end date in November 2015.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-110) By the thousandth day of the program, before Buttigieg's first term ended, nearly 40 percent of the targeted houses were repaired, and 679 were demolished or under contract for demolition.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-111) Buttigieg took note of the fact that many homes within communities of color were the ones demolished, leading to early distrust between the city and these communities.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-112)

While mayor, Buttigieg served for seven months in Afghanistan as a lieutenant in the [U.S. Navy Reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy_Reserve "United States Navy Reserve"), returning to the United States on September 23, 2014.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Bell-113) In his absence, Deputy Mayor Mark Neal, South Bend's city [comptroller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comptroller#United_States "Comptroller"), served as executive from February 2014 until Buttigieg returned to his role as mayor in October 2014.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Fuller-2014-88)[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Bell-113)[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-114)

In 2015, during the controversy over [Indiana Senate Bill 101](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religious_Freedom_Restoration_Act_(Indiana) "Religious Freedom Restoration Act (Indiana)") – the original version of which was widely criticized for allowing discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender people – Buttigieg emerged as a leading opponent of the legislation. Amid his reelection campaign, he [came out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coming_out "Coming out") as [gay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homosexuality "Homosexuality") and expressed his solidarity with the LGBTQ community.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Buttigieg-2015-115)[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-116)

### Second term

Buttigieg announced in 2014 that he would seek a second term in [2015](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_South_Bend_mayoral_election "2015 South Bend mayoral election").[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-southbendvoice-102) He won the [Democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") primary with approximately 78 percent of the vote, defeating Henry Davis Jr., the city councilman from the second district.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-117) In November 2015, he was elected to his second term as mayor with over 80 percent of the vote, defeating Republican Kelly Jones by a margin of 8,515 to 2,074 votes.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-118) After winning reelection, Buttigieg signed an executive order helping to establish a recognized [city identification card](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_identification_card "City identification card") in 2016.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-119)[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-120)

To improve South Bend's downtown area, Buttigieg proposed a Smart Streets urban development program in 2013.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-South_Bend_Tribune-2018-92) In early 2015 – after traffic studies and public hearings – he secured a [bond issue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bond_issue "Bond issue") for the program backed by [tax increment financing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_increment_financing "Tax increment financing").[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-121)[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Parrott-2018-122) Smart Streets was a [complete streets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete_streets "Complete streets") implementation program[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-123) aimed at improving economic development and urban vibrancy as well as road safety.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Buttigieg-2017-124) Elements of the project were finished in 2016,[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-South_Bend_Tribune-2018-92) and the project was officially completed in 2017.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Buttigieg-2017-124) The project was credited with spurring private development in the city.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Parrott-2018-122)

In a new phase of the Vacant and Abandoned Properties Initiative, South Bend partnered with the Notre Dame Clinical Law Center to provide free legal assistance to qualifying applicants wishing to acquire vacant lots and, with local nonprofits, to repair or construct homes and provide low-income home ownership assistance using South Bend [Housing and Urban Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Housing_and_Urban_Development "Housing and Urban Development") funds.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-125)[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-126)

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/CN_Train%2C_Former_Studebaker_Factory_%2815100168261%29.jpg/250px-CN_Train%2C_Former_Studebaker_Factory_%2815100168261%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CN_Train,_Former_Studebaker_Factory_(15100168261).jpg)Studebaker Building 84 in 2014

The City of South Bend partnered with the State of Indiana and private developers to break ground on a $165-million renovation of the former [Studebaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studebaker "Studebaker") complex in 2016, hoping that the redevelopment would facilitate industrial and housing units.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Colombo-2017-127) This development is in the Renaissance District which includes nearby Ignition Park.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Gardner-2019-128) In 2017, it was announced that the long-abandoned Studebaker Building 84, also known as *Ivy Tower*, would have its exterior renovated with $3.5 million in Regional Cities funds from the State of Indiana and another $3.5 million from South Bend tax increment financing, with plans for the building and other structures in its complex to serve as a technology hub.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-129) The website *Best Cities* later ranked South Bend number 39 on its 2020 list of the 100 best small cities in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), citing Buttigieg's efforts to revitalize the Studebaker factory and Downtown South Bend.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-130)

Under Buttigieg, the city also began a smart sewer program, the first phase of which was finished in 2017 at a cost of $150 million.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Gardner-2019-128) The effort used federal funds[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-131) and by 2019 had reduced the combined sewer overflow by 75 percent.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Gardner-2019-128) The impetus for the effort was a fine that the EPA had levied against the city in 2011 for [Clean Water Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clean_Water_Act "Clean Water Act") violations.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Gardner-2019-128) In 2019, Buttigieg asked for the city to be released from an agreement with the EPA brokered under his mayoral predecessor Steve Luecke, in which South Bend had agreed to make hundreds of millions of dollars in further improvements to its sewer system by 2031.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-132)

The Common Council approved Buttigieg's request to enable his administration to develop a city climate plan in April 2019; Buttigieg signed a contract with the Chicago firm Delta Institute to help develop it.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-133) In late November 2019, the city's Common Council voted 7–0 to approve the resultant Carbon Neutral 2050 plan, setting the goal of meeting the Paris Agreement's 26-percent emission reduction by 2025, and aiming for a further reductions of 45 percent by 2035.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-134)

Supporting private development in South Bend was another initiative Buttigieg continued during his second term.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-135)[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-136)[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-137)[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-138)[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-139) By 2019, the city had seen $374 million in private investment for [mixed-use developments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed-use_development "Mixed-use development") since Buttigieg had taken office, by one estimate.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-140)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Sikich-2019-101) By another account, Downtown South Bend saw roughly $200 million in private investment during Buttigieg's tenure.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-141)

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/20041231_14_NICTD_South_Bend%2C_IN_%288873027699%29.jpg/250px-20041231_14_NICTD_South_Bend%2C_IN_%288873027699%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:20041231_14_NICTD_South_Bend,_IN_(8873027699).jpg)In 2018, Buttigieg proposed moving the city's [South Shore Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Shore_Line "South Shore Line") [station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Bend_International_Airport_station "South Bend International Airport station"), from the airport to downtown.

With respect to infrastructure, Buttigieg promoted [the idea of moving the city's South Shore Line station from South Bend International Airport to the city's downtown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proposed_South_Shore_Line_station_in_South_Bend "Proposed South Shore Line station in South Bend") in August 2018.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-142) He made it a goal to have the city complete this project by 2025.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-143) Also, South Bend launched Commuters Trust, a new [transportation benefit program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Employer_transportation_benefits_in_the_United_States "Employer transportation benefits in the United States") created in collaboration with local employers and transportation providers, including [South Bend Transpo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Bend_Transpo "South Bend Transpo") and [Lyft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyft "Lyft"), in 2019. The program was made possible by a $1 million three-year grant from [Bloomberg Philanthropies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomberg_Philanthropies "Bloomberg Philanthropies") Mayors Challenge.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-144)[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-145) Furthermore, under Buttigieg, South Bend invested $50 million in the city's parks, many of which had been neglected during the preceding decades.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Sikich-2019-101)

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f1/Black_Lives_Matter_Rally_20200605064_%2849975052738%29.jpg/250px-Black_Lives_Matter_Rally_20200605064_%2849975052738%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Black_Lives_Matter_Rally_20200605064_(49975052738).jpg)Protestors marching in response to the death of Eric Logan

After a white South Bend police officer shot and killed Eric Logan, an African American man, in June 2019, Buttigieg was drawn from his presidential campaign to focus on the emerging public reaction. Police body cameras were not turned on during Logan's death.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-146) Soon after Logan's death, Buttigieg presided over a [town hall meeting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Town_hall_meeting "Town hall meeting") attended by disaffected activists from the African American community as well as relatives of the deceased man. The local police union accused Buttigieg of making decisions for political gain.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-147)[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-148) Buttigieg secured $180,000 in November 2019 to commission a review of South Bend's police department policies and practices, to be conducted by Chicago-based consulting firm 21CP Solutions.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-149)

Some African Americans have accused Buttigieg of racism for his response to this and other incidents. Former South Bend councilman Henry Davis Jr. alleged that Buttigieg "perpetuated and tolerated" systemic racism in the city. Michael Harriot, senior writer at [The Root](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Root_(magazine) "The Root (magazine)"), accused Buttigieg of "racist paternalism" for saying that children of color lack role models that promote the value of education. Many African Americans also point to Buttigieg's firing of Darryl Boykins, South Bend's first black chief of police. Boykins claimed that Buttigieg used a scandal—involving secret tapes of white police officers making racist comments—as a pretext for firing him.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-150)[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-151)[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-152)

#### Increased national profile

In the [2016 U.S. Senate election in Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_Senate_election_in_Indiana "2016 United States Senate election in Indiana"), he campaigned on behalf of [Democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") Senate nominee [Evan Bayh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evan_Bayh "Evan Bayh")[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-153) and criticized Bayh's opponent, [Todd Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Todd_Young "Todd Young"), for having voiced support in 2010 for retaining the military's [don't ask, don't tell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don't_ask,_don't_tell "Don't ask, don't tell") policy, which Bayh had [voted to repeal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don't_Ask,_Don't_Tell_Repeal_Act_of_2010 "Don't Ask, Don't Tell Repeal Act of 2010").[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-154) In the [2016 Democratic presidential primaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Democratic_Party_presidential_primaries "2016 Democratic Party presidential primaries"), Buttigieg endorsed [Hillary Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillary_Clinton "Hillary Clinton").[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-155) He also endorsed Democratic nominee Lynn Coleman in [that year's election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections_in_Indiana#District_2 "2016 United States House of Representatives elections in Indiana") for [Indiana's 2nd congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana's_2nd_congressional_district "Indiana's 2nd congressional district"), which included South Bend.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-156)

[Frank Bruni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Bruni "Frank Bruni") of *[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")* published a 2016 column praising Buttigieg's work as mayor, with a headline asking if he might be "the first gay president".[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Bruni-2016-157) [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") cited him as one of the Democratic Party's talents in a November 2016 profile on the outgoing president conducted by *[The New Yorker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_Yorker "The New Yorker")*.[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-158) As Buttigieg's national profile grew following his run in the [2017 Democratic National Committee chairmanship election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Democratic_National_Committee_chairmanship_election "2017 Democratic National Committee chairmanship election"), Buttigieg increased his out-of-city travel.[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-159) By early 2018, there was speculation that Buttigieg would run for either governor or president in 2020.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-160)[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-161)

For the [2018 midterms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_United_States_elections "2018 United States elections"), Buttigieg founded the political action committee (PAC) [Hitting Home PAC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hitting_Home_PAC "Hitting Home PAC").[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-162) That October, Buttigieg personally endorsed 21 congressional candidates.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Wren-2018a-163) He also later endorsed Mel Hall, Democratic nominee in [the 2018 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections_in_Indiana#District_2 "2018 United States House of Representatives elections in Indiana") for Indiana's 2nd congressional district.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-164) Buttigieg campaigned for Joe Donnelly's reelection campaign in the [United States Senate election in Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_United_States_Senate_election_in_Indiana "2018 United States Senate election in Indiana").[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-165) Buttigieg campaigned for candidates in more than a dozen states, including early presidential primary states such as [Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iowa "Iowa") and [South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Carolina "South Carolina"), a move indicating potential interest in running for president.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-Wren-2018a-163) He officially announced his run on January 23, 2019.[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Buttigieg#cite_note-166)

#### Succession as mayor
